title: Significance of the Study (With Examples) | AnswerThis
summary: The significance of the study explains who benefits from your findings and how. Learn to write it in four steps, with six examples in two formats.
body_markdown:
The significance of the study is the part of a research paper that explains who will benefit from your findings and how. It answers the question every panel eventually asks: why does this study matter, and to whom?


This page explains where the section goes, how it differs from the parts around it, and how to write it in four steps. It then gives six examples from different fields, each written in the two formats schools most often ask for.


## TL;DR


-


The significance of the study names who benefits from the findings and what each group can do with them.


-


In many Philippine theses it sits in Chapter 1, after the statement of the problem and any hypotheses.


-


You can organize it by beneficiary or by contribution to theory, practice and policy.


-


Keep the claims modest, since one study rarely changes a whole system.


## Where does the significance of the study go?


In many Philippine theses, the significance of the study is part of Chapter 1. It usually comes after the statement of the problem and any[hypotheses](https://answerthis.io/blog/how-to-write-a-hypothesis) , and before the scope and delimitation. In a research proposal it plays the same role, telling the reader why the project deserves approval, and our guide on[how to write a research proposal](https://answerthis.io/blog/how-to-write-a-compelling-research-proposal) covers the sections around it.


Do not confuse it with statistical significance. Statistical significance is a technical result from a statistical test, usually a p-value below a chosen cutoff. The[American Statistical Association's statement on p-values](https://doi.org/10.1080/00031305.2016.1154108) notes that a p-value does not measure how important a result is. The significance of the study is about importance: what the findings could mean for real people.


## How is it different from the background, rationale and scope?


These sections sit close together in Chapter 1, and students often repeat themselves across them. Each one answers a different question.


Section


The question it answers


Background of the study


What is already known about the problem and its setting?


Rationale


Why is this study needed now?


Significance of the study


Who will benefit from the findings, and how?


Scope and delimitation


What will the study cover, and what will it leave out?


## How do you write the significance of the study?


1.


Start from the problem. Reread your statement of the problem and research questions, since the significance should grow out of them. If your questions are still vague, our[research question examples](https://answerthis.io/blog/research-question-examples) can help you sharpen them first.


2.


Say what the findings add. Name the specific knowledge, evidence or tool the study will produce.


3.


Name who benefits and how. For each group, give a concrete use of the findings, not just a label.


4.


Keep the claims modest. Use “may help” or “can inform” rather than “will solve.”


Here is the difference the last step makes. “This study will improve education in the Philippines” promises more than any single study can deliver. “The findings may help Grade 7 English teachers decide whether peer tutoring is worth class time” is specific, believable and easy for a panel to accept.


## Which format should you use?


Most significance sections follow one of two formats.


-


By beneficiary. One short paragraph for each group that can use the findings, such as students, teachers, parents, administrators, policymakers and future researchers.


-


By contribution. One short paragraph each on what the study adds to theory, to practice and to policy.


Undergraduate theses in the Philippines often use the beneficiary format, while graduate theses and journal articles more often describe contributions. Your research manual or adviser decides, which is why each example below shows both.


## Significance of the study examples


### 1. Education


*Study: Effects of Peer Tutoring on the Reading Comprehension of Grade 7 Learners in a Public High School*


By beneficiary: Learners may gain a low-cost way to improve their reading. English teachers will have evidence on whether peer tutoring is worth class time. School heads can use the results when planning reading programs, and future researchers can test the approach in other grade levels.


By contribution: In practice, the study tests a reading strategy that needs no extra materials. For policy, it gives schools local evidence for choosing reading interventions. For theory, it adds Philippine classroom data to research on peer learning.


### 2. Nursing


*Study: Factors Affecting Medication Adherence Among Older Adults With Hypertension in a Rural Health Unit*


By beneficiary: Patients and their families may better understand what keeps them from taking medicines as prescribed. Nurses and barangay health workers can use the findings to focus their counseling. Rural health unit administrators can plan follow-up visits, and future researchers can extend the study to other chronic conditions.


By contribution: In practice, it points nurses to the barriers that matter most locally. For policy, it can inform community programs for hypertension. For theory, it tests whether known adherence factors hold among older Filipino patients.


### 3. Business


*Study: Digital Payment Adoption Among Sari-Sari Store Owners in Quezon City*


By beneficiary: Store owners can learn which concerns others had before accepting e-wallet payments. Digital payment providers may use the findings to simplify onboarding. Local business offices can tailor support for micro-enterprises, and future researchers gain a baseline for other cities.


By contribution: In practice, it identifies the barriers providers and owners can address. For policy, it can inform financial inclusion efforts for small retailers. For theory, it applies technology acceptance models to small, family-run businesses.


### 4. Information technology


*Study: Development and Usability Testing of a Mobile Attendance System for a State University*


By beneficiary: Students may spend less class time on roll calls and get more accurate attendance records. Faculty members can track attendance with fewer errors. The registrar can check records in real time, and future developers can reuse the design and test results.


By contribution: In practice, it delivers a working system with a usability evaluation. For policy, it can support a campus move to digital records. For method, it shows how a standard measure such as the System Usability Scale can be applied in a Philippine campus setting.


### 5. Social science


*Study: Lived Experiences of Adolescent Children of Overseas Filipino Workers*


By beneficiary: OFW families may better understand how separation affects their children. Guidance counselors and teachers can use the findings to support these students. Local social welfare offices can design programs for families left behind, and future researchers can compare experiences across regions.


By contribution: For theory, it adds adolescents' own voices to research on families separated by migration. In practice, it gives counselors concrete issues to address. For policy, it can inform support services for OFW families.


### 6. Environmental science


*Study: Household Solid Waste Segregation Practices in a Coastal Barangay*


By beneficiary: Residents may see where their segregation habits fall short. Barangay officials can target information drives and collection schedules. Municipal environment offices can use the data when enforcing waste rules, and future researchers can compare coastal and inland communities.


By contribution: In practice, it shows which households need the most support. For policy, it can inform local implementation of the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000 (Republic Act 9003). For theory, it adds data on the gap between what residents know about segregation and what they do.


## What are the most common mistakes?


-


Overclaiming. Promising that a study will solve poverty or reform a national program makes a panel doubt the rest of the chapter.


-


Naming beneficiaries without a reason. “This study will benefit parents” says nothing until you explain what parents can do with the findings.


-


Repeating the background. The significance should look forward to what the findings make possible, not restate the problem.


-


Listing everyone. If you cannot say how a group would use the results, leave that group out.


## FAQs


### How long should the significance of the study be?


Usually a few paragraphs, often one short paragraph per beneficiary or contribution. Follow your school's manual, and cut any group you cannot give a specific reason for.


### Should it be written in the future tense?


In a proposal, usually yes, since the study has not been done yet. Use “will” for what the study will produce and “may” for benefits you cannot guarantee. Some schools ask you to revise the tense in the final thesis.


### Do I need citations in the significance of the study?


Not usually, because the section is about your own study. Cite a source when you state a fact, such as a policy, a statistic or a gap another study identified.


### What order should the beneficiaries go in?


Many writers start with the group most directly affected and end with future researchers. If your manual sets an order, use that instead.


### Is the significance of the study the same as the rationale?


No. The rationale explains why the study is needed, while the significance explains who will benefit from its findings. They are closely related, so check that the two sections do not repeat each other.


If you are drafting the whole proposal, start from the AnswerThis[research proposal template](https://answerthis.io/template/research-proposal) , then write your significance of the study last, once your problem and questions are settled.
